extracted.intended_audience: architects, art historians, students and educated general readers evaluating or learning to recognise Gothic architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and stylistic rules for identifying, judging, and distinguishing good Gothic architecture (forms, ornament, construction, and relative quality across periods/regions). Focuses on roof/arch forms, foliation/tracery, structural soundness, and distinctions between early/late and surface/linear Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final definition of Gothic
rubrics_metrics.description: "Foliated Architecture, which uses the pointed arch for the roof proper, and the gable for the roof-mask."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is given as the concise, final test: Gothic architecture must show foliation and combine the pointed arch (as the structural coverage) with the gable as the visible roof-mask. The surrounding discussion explains that foliation may appear in arches or apertures and is an essential character of the style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foliation is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: "No Gothic is either good or characteristic which is not foliated either in its arches or apertures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The element of foliation (cusps, traceries, foliated openings) must enter somewhere in the design; if absent the building is not good/characteristic Gothic. Foliation can appear in bearing arches or in apertures above them; one or the other suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointed arches and gables united
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal windows and doors should have pointed arches with gables over them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: if windows/doors lack pointed arches the building is not Gothic; if they lack gables over them it is either not pure Gothic or not first-rate. If steep roof, pointed arch, and gable are all united, it is nearly certain to be a fine Gothic building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roof must rise in a steep gable
rubrics_metrics.description: "Look if the roof rises in a steep gable, high above the walls."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First plain practical rule for determining Gothic: absence of a steep gable roof indicates the building is not quite pure Gothic or has been altered. The roof-mask (gable) relationship to the roof proper is fundamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gable steepness semicircle test
rubrics_metrics.description: If you strike a semicircle on the base of a gable: if its top rises above the semicircle it is Gothic; if it falls beneath it is Romanesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple practical geometric test to distinguish Gothic (steep/acute gable) from Romanesque (low/obtuse gable). The best forms in each group are distinctly steep or distinctly low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of separation of gable angles
rubrics_metrics.description: A Gothic gable must have all its angles acute; a Romanesque one will have the upper one obtuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctive rule: the slope and angle relationships of the gable separate Northern (acute) and Southern (flat/obtuse) traditions; used to classify and judge authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three generic roofing solutions (architectural taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: All ways of bridging a space reduce to three: a lintel, the round arch, and the gable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this follows the classification of three 'good' architectures: A Greek (lintel), B Romanesque (round arch), C Gothic (gable). Purity of an architecture is proportional to the simplicity/directness with which it expresses its roofing principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build pointed arches in the strongest manner (structural criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all possible forms of the pointed arch (given a certain weight of material), the form with thickened flanks and cusps (generic form represented at e) is the strongest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural guidance: pointed arches are weak at their flanks; thickening these or adding cusps prevents fracture. The text uses diagram examples to show how forms c, d, e behave under loads. Good Gothic follows structural logic where possible, not mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cusp advantage and scale limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The structural advantage of the cusp is available only on a comparatively small scale; very large arches cannot employ heavy cusps safely and must rely on mass and/or tracery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design guidance: on small arches cusps add strength and beauty; on large spans use general mass of masonry and tracery to obtain apparent support. This is a constraint when judging appropriateness of cusped forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracery and foliation origin and desirable character
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracery began as penetrations cut into stonework forming star-like shapes indoors and leaf-like shapes outdoors; the best traceries are close clusters of such foils with mouldings following their outlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good tracery should combine geometrical order and radiated leaf-like forms (foils). Effective traceries are not random cuttings but deliberate clusters respecting symmetry and outline; they connect ornament with structural apertures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foliation must be invented or accurately copied (anti‑pattern: random foliation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foliation is an easy method of decoration and can be abused: 'Throw any number of crossing lines together at random... and you will immediately have what will stand, with most people, for very satisfactory Gothic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: superficial or random foliation produces commonplace, uninventive Gothic. Floral decoration and moulding disposition require real thought and invention; mere random patterns indicate ignoble imitation, not true architectural merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between early (noble) and late (ignoble) Gothic
rubrics_metrics.description: Two vast schools: the early (noble, inventive, progressive) uses foliation moderately and floral/figure sculpture profusely; the late (ignoble, uninventive, declining) uses foliation immoderately and floral/figure sculpture subordinately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a quality/time criterion: early Gothic balances foliation and sculpture, showing invention and vigour; late Gothic over-relies on lace-like traceries and repeats the same idea, indicating decline. Examples: southern (Italian/Veronese) versus northern (French) tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface-Gothic (Linear-Gothic) distinction and value judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface-Gothic (Italian/Veronese) is strong in masonry, simple in mass, and perpetual in variety; Linear-Gothic (late French/traceried) is weak in masonry, broken in mass, and repetitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging works, prefer Surface-Gothic for structural nobility and permanence; Linear-Gothic may be very beautiful in line but is inferior in masonry strength and compositional robustness. Use examples (Verona tomb vs Abbeville door) to compare treatment of foliation and sculpture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition robustness principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A composition from which anything can be removed without doing mischief is always so far forth inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General artistic criterion: architectural composition should be such that all elements are essential; if the work sustains removal of parts without harm, it lacks integrity and therefore is of lower merit. Applied to Gothic: late traceried work often can lose sculpture without damage, evidence of inferiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association of gable and arch may invert during transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: In transitional passages between styles one sometimes finds pointed arches under low gables or round arches under high gables (reversed conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize transitional/ hybrid forms (e.g., tombs of Verona or doors of Venice) when evaluating purity or period: inversion is possible and informative about regional/developmental phases rather than simple 'good/bad' labeling.
